ann_90.text: In this straight-line part, more daytime minutes clearly raise the predicted chance steadily, for a typical customer from below 1% at 112 minutes to about 24% at 249 minutes, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower, and an international plan clearly raises it from about 2% to about 17%.
More evening and night-time minutes and higher evening and international charges each raise it steadily but only slightly, and a voice-mail plan changes it only slightly.

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted chance only slightly (on the training data only): a higher daytime charge, more voice-mail messages, a longer account and more daytime calls each raise it steadily; more evening calls lower it steadily; more night-time calls barely change it; area codes 408 and 510 lower it a little; and the state shifts it by a few points at most, from below 1% in Hawaii and Vermont to about 5% in California, Maryland and Arkansas.

ann_91.original: Low-usage x customer-service-calls gate. Node 807 = relu(-1.2 - 1.39 dayMin + 0.87*h2627 + 0.72*h2796 ...) is a hinge that is ON for low day minutes; its knot moves up with service calls (CSC enters via 13061->12926->2796 and 9555->2627) and with low eve charge / low night minutes (2796, 12926) and voicemail plan (9555). 1264 = relu(0.12 - 0.31 intlCharge + 0.43*807) amplifies 807, more for low international charge. Readout 1.68*807 + 1.92*1264 (+0.38*12809, which is dead: 12809 = relu(-0.78 - 0.54*h2796) is 0 on every row since h2796 >= 0). Its mean slope in day minutes (-2.31/z) cancels the backbone's +2.75/z, so the network's logit is V-shaped in day minutes, with the low-usage arm raised by about +1.8, +4.5, +6 logits at CSC = 4, 5, 6 relative to CSC <= 3. Evidence (train): gate logit by CSC x dayMin bins rises with CSC (CSC0 lowest-usage bin 8.64, CSC4 12.85, CSC6 13.22) and falls with dayMin; full-model partial dependence over dayMin is V-shaped with the low arm lifted by CSC (min logit -3.85 at CSC0, -1.50 at CSC4, +1.31 at CSC6). Empirical churn for CSC>=4 is 1.00/0.96/0.86 in the three lowest dayMin bins vs ~0.05 for CSC<4, matching. Performance: linearising this child alone drops AUC 0.908 -> 0.839; restoring it alone onto the fully linearised model gives 0.905 of the 0.908. It also contains a rare-category switch: state:20 (82 rows) zeroes node 2796, removing the CSC/eve-charge path (logit effects -5.1 to +1.1 per row).
ann_91.proposed: For customers with daytime minutes below about 206 and an evening charge below about $20, this part raises the predicted chance, more so with a voice-mail plan; customer-service calls add slightly.

Evidence (train): contribution 0 for <=3 calls, +0.41/+0.77/+1.22/+1.47 for 4/5/6/7 calls; churn rate 0.11 for <=3 calls vs 0.44/0.57/0.68 for 4/5/6. ann_97.original: Root: churn logit = -1.19 + linear_backbone + csc_usage_gate + csc_hinge + eve_state_hinge + intl_calls_hinge + night_charge_hinge + category_offsets, output = sigmoid(logit). Purely additive composition of the seven children at the output node. 21 inputs (19 state one-hots, areaCode:408, totalIntlMinutes) are unconnected (zero-effect entries). The performance comes almost entirely from csc_usage_gate: linearising all nonlinear children drops train AUC 0.908 -> 0.831; restoring csc_usage_gate alone gives 0.905. summary.text: For a typical customer (in West Virginia, area code 415, with no international or voice-mail plan, one call to customer service and median usage, such as about 180 daytime minutes), having an international plan clearly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 2% to about 17%.

Across the whole model, more evening minutes raise it only slightly, quickly at first and then levelling off; going from 0 to 3 customer-service calls raises it only slightly, in an uneven way across customers; and a voice-mail plan lowers it only slightly.

Inside the model, daytime minutes clearly pull in two directions: as they go from 112 to 249, one part raises the predicted chance steadily, from below 1% to about 24%, while another lowers it in an uneven way, from about 57% to about 1%.

That second part clearly matters only while daytime minutes stay below about 206 (between 171 and 253 minutes for different customers): going from 91 to 352 minutes lowers the predicted chance for a typical customer in an uneven way, from about 84% to about 1%.
A higher daytime charge and more voice-mail messages raise it steadily but only slightly, and the state changes it only slightly, with California the largest at about 5% (on the training data only).
The model ignores total international minutes.

parts.name: csc_hinge
parts.original_hypothesis: 7208 = relu(-0.52 + 0.43*CSC - 0.44*state:49), readout 1.21: a hinge in number of customer service calls that switches on at about 3 calls (z ~ 1.1) and adds about +0.52 logit per further z-unit (~+0.4 per call); the state:49 one-hot (z ~ 6) switches it off. Evidence (train): contribution 0 for <=3 calls, +0.41/+0.77/+1.22/+1.47 for 4/5/6/7 calls; churn rate 0.11 for <=3 calls vs 0.44/0.57/0.68 for 4/5/6. parts.name: intl_calls_hinge
parts.original_hypothesis: 4967 = relu(1.75 + 0.9*state:8 + 1.46*intlCalls) -> 7647 = relu(-1.83 + 0.96*h4967) -> 10249 = relu(0.16 + 0.98*state:3 - 1.13*h7647), readouts 0.01*7647 + 0.10*10249. parts.name: night_charge_hinge
parts.original_hypothesis: 8896 = relu(-0.16 - 0.70*nightCharge), readout -0.26: lowers churn logit for customers with low night charge (z < -0.23), i.e. it steepens the backbone's night-usage slope (+0.45/z) to about +0.63/z at the low end. reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

ann_91.text: This part acts on 3552 of 4000 training customers (89%).
For a typical customer it acts on, it slightly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from below 1% without this part to about 2% with it.
In the training data, 450 of these 3552 customers had churn.

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: a higher total international charge lowers it in an uneven way; total night-time minutes past about 163 minutes lowers it in an uneven way; South Dakota (rather than any other state) raises it; a higher customer-service calls raises it in an uneven way; a higher total night-time minutes lowers it in an uneven way; Maryland (rather than any other state) lowers it; total evening charge depending on state raises it steadily; a higher total daytime calls raises it steadily; and one still smaller effect listed in the evidence table (on the training data only).

summary.text: For a typical customer, the model gives a clearly higher predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer has an international plan (about 17%) than if the customer has no international plan (about 2%).

Through one part of the model, total daytime minutes only clearly lowers the predicted chance that a customer leaves while it stays below about 206 minutes (between 171 minutes and 253 minutes for different customers): for a typical such customer, going from 91 minutes to 352 minutes moves it from about 84% to about 1%; across patients the change happens in an uneven way.

Through one part of the model, total evening charge only clearly lowers the predicted chance that a customer leaves while it stays below about 20.43 US dollars (between 10.35 US dollars and 22.66 US dollars for different customers): for a typical such customer, going from 10.13 US dollars to 30.91 US dollars moves it from about 23% to about 1%; across patients the change happens in an uneven way.
The model ignores total international minutes.
